- They value aesthetics and want products that fit into a modern home.
- They are willing to pay more for quality if they trust the brand.
- They trust peer recommendations and reviews more than ads.

2. Content pillars

Product features: each product gets its own look. Show it in use in a real home. If it's made from recycled materials, say so and show the material.

Education: explain what makes the product eco-friendly. For example, if it's made from recycled glass, explain what that means for waste and energy. If it's plastic-free or biodegradable, explain why that matters. If it's long-lasting, explain how a product that lasts longer means fewer replacements.

User-generated content (UGC): real customers using the products in their own homes.

Behind the scenes: how the product is made, who makes it, and what you're working on next.

3. Content calendar (four weeks)

Week 1: launch

Day 1: announcement post, big image, short video of the collection.

Day 3: product spotlight post, one item.

Day 5: educational post, what makes the collection eco-friendly.

Day 7: UGC post, repost a customer photo.

Week 2: education

Day 1: educational deep dive, why it matters.

Day 3: product spotlight, second item.

Day 5: "how to use it" short video.

Day 7: customer review post.

Week 3: community

Day 1: UGC, customer photos of the product in their homes.

Day 3: educational post, how to make your home more sustainable.

Day 5: product spotlight, third item.

Day 7: behind the scenes, how it's made.

Week 4: conversion

Day 1: limited-time offer or new arrival.

Day 3: educational post, common eco-friendly myths.

Day 5: UGC, customer testimonials.

Day 7: wrap-up and what's next.

Post frequency: on Instagram and TikTok, aim for one post a day and three to five Stories a day. On Facebook, two to three posts a week is enough. On Pinterest, pin the product images every day.

4. Visual style

Use natural light, real home settings, and warm tones. The images should feel lived in, not like a studio shoot. Use short, upbeat videos with a calm voiceover, and make sure the product is the focus. Include text overlays on videos with the key selling point.

5. Influencer and blogger collaboration

Influencers:

Micro-influencers (10,000 to 100,000 followers), especially lifestyle and home decor accounts, give the best return. Their followers trust them and engage more.

Send them a free product before they commit. Ask them to show the product in their own home, not just hold it in a studio.

Ask for a discount code for their followers, with a commission on sales.

Have them post a Story with a Question sticker so followers can ask about the product.

Eco-friendly bloggers:

Write guest posts for them on how to make your home more sustainable, with the products mentioned naturally.

Pitch the collection as a story for them to cover, with press images.

Sponsor their newsletter.

Example outreach message:

"Hi [name], I love your post on [topic]. My name is [name], and I'm launching an eco-friendly home accessory line. I'd love to send you some pieces to try at home. No pressure, just wanted to share! Here's what we're about: [one sentence]."

6. Conversion plan

In the first week, drive traffic to a landing page with the collection, an "about" section, and a newsletter sign-up with a 10% off code.

Use Instagram Shopping and Facebook Shop so products are shoppable.

Run a giveaway: follow the account, tag two friends, and post a photo with the product. This builds followers and UGC.

Retargeting: use Meta Pixel and TikTok Pixel to retarget people who visited the site but didn't buy, with a discount code.

Email: send a welcome email, a "how to use it" email, and a review request email after the product arrives.

7. Key performance indicators (KPIs)

Reach:

- Follower growth rate: (new followers / total followers) x 100, measured every two weeks.

- Reach and impressions: how many people saw the posts.

Engagement:

- Engagement rate: (likes + comments + shares + saves) / reach x 100.

- Story engagement: replies, poll votes, and question sticker responses.

- UGC volume: how many posts mention the brand or use the campaign hashtag.

Traffic:

- Referral traffic from social media: Google Analytics, by source.

- Landing page visits and sign-ups.

Conversion:

- Sales conversion rate: (sales / site visits) x 100.

- Revenue per post: revenue / impressions x 100,000.

- Influencer code usage and sales per influencer.

After the four weeks, review and adjust. Look at which posts had the highest engagement and why. Look at which influencers drove the most traffic and sales. Look at the KPIs and adjust the plan for the next month accordingly.

prompt: Provide a step-by-step guide on how to care for a wool rug, including the frequency of vacuuming and how to properly spot clean any stains that may occur. Include information on what type of vacuum to use, how to avoid damaging the fibers while vacuuming, and what to do if a spill occurs on the rug. Additionally, provide tips on how to maintain the wool rug's softness and prevent any damage from sunlight or high traffic areas.
completion:
Wool is one of the most durable natural fibres, but it does need regular care. Left alone, the pile will crush in the paths where you walk, the dust will grind into the fibres and abrade them, and spills will set into permanent stains. A simple routine will keep it soft and looking new for years.

Vacuuming

How often: Vacuum high-traffic areas two or three times a week, and other areas once a week. In homes with pets or children, increase the frequency, because dirt and crumbs are the main cause of wear.

The right vacuum: Use one with a suction-only head or one where the brush roll can be turned off. A motorised brush head that spins rapidly will pull at the pile and can damage delicate or loosely knotted rugs. If your vacuum has a "hard floor" or "bargain" setting, that usually means the brush roll is disabled. If it doesn't, use a suction-only attachment.

How to vacuum:
1. Shake out the rug outside every few months. This removes the heavy, gritty dirt that causes wear before you even vacuum.
2. Vacuum slowly, with long overlapping strokes, and change direction each pass so you pick up dirt from all angles.
3. Don't press down hard. Let the suction do the work.
4. Vacuum the edges and fringes gently with the upholstery or crevice tool. Don't vacuum the fringe aggressively, as this can pull loose the fringe knots.
5. Move furniture occasionally and vacuum underneath it, because the crushed pile under heavy legs takes a long time to recover.

Spot cleaning spills

Act quickly. The sooner you treat a spill, the better the chances of removing it completely.

What to use:
- Clean, lukewarm water. For most spills, this is all you need.
- A mild detergent made for wool or a carpet, such as one with a pH of 7 to 8. You can also use a very mild dish soap diluted heavily (about half a teaspoon per cup of water).
- A clean white cloth or sponge. Never use a coloured cloth, which can bleed.
- A small amount of white vinegar for acidic stains, like wine, coffee or fruit juice.

How to clean a spot:
1. Blot up as much of the liquid as possible with a clean, dry cloth. Press down. Don't rub. Rubbing spreads the stain and works it deeper into the fibres.
2. Mix your cleaning solution. Test it on a small, hidden area of the rug first, such as under a sofa, to make sure it doesn't discolor or damage the wool.
3. Dampen (don't soak) the cloth in the solution and blot the stain from the outside edge toward the centre. Changing direction prevents the stain from spreading.
4. Rinse by blotting with a cloth dampened with clean water.
5. Blot dry with a clean, dry towel.
6. Lay a dry towel over the spot and weigh it down with a book. Leave it for several hours or overnight.
7. Once dry, fluff the pile with your fingers or a stiff brush.

Avoid these:
- Bleach or strong chemical cleaners, which can damage the fibres.
- Vinegar on protein stains, such as milk, blood or urine. Vinegar is acidic and can set these stains into the wool. Use a mild detergent instead.
- Heat, which can shrink or felt wool.

Stains that are stubborn or don't respond to home treatment should be handled by a professional rug cleaner who understands wool.

Maintaining softness

- Rotate the rug every three to six months so that the areas exposed to the most foot traffic get a break and wear evenly.
- Gently brush the pile with a soft bristle brush or a carpet rake after vacuuming and again a few days later. This helps the fibres stand up and keeps the rug feeling soft.
- Avoid heavy furniture with narrow legs resting on the same spot for long periods. Use furniture pads to spread the weight more evenly.
- Keep the rug out of reach of pets' claws, or trim their nails regularly.

Protecting against sunlight

Wool dye can fade when exposed to direct sunlight over time, so:
- Use curtains or blinds on windows that get strong direct sun.
- Place rugs away from sunny windows where possible. If that isn't feasible, consider using a UV-protective window film.
- Rotate the rug regularly so that no single section gets more sun than the rest.

Protecting high traffic areas

- Use runners or mats in entryways, hallways and staircases to protect the rug from the heaviest traffic.
- If the rug is in a high-traffic area, consider having it professionally cleaned once a year to remove deep dirt before it grinds into the fibres.
- Trim any loose threads with scissors. Don't pull on them, as that can unravel the knot.

If you follow these steps, your wool rug will retain its softness, colour and integrity for many years.
